summary: An edition of the IAB Official Protocol Standards, a periodic list of the standardization status of Internet protocols. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1410.

plainLanguage.summary: A regularly updated report card listing which protocols are official and how far each has come in the standards process.

subtitle: The official status and maturity of Internet protocols

tldr.problem: The Internet has many protocols at different stages of development and adoption. Systems need a clear, authoritative way to know which protocols are official, how mature they are, and when they should use them.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board publishes an official list classifying each protocol by its maturity level (standard, draft standard, proposed standard, experimental, informational, or historic) and its requirement level (required, recommended, elective, limited use, or not recommended).
tldr.outcome: This RFC itself is historic, replaced by RFC 1410, but the classification system it describes remains fundamental to Internet standards processes.

today: RFC 1360 is historic and was replaced by RFC 1410. However, the protocol classification scheme it describes—maturity levels (standard, draft standard, proposed standard, experimental, informational, historic) and requirement levels (required, recommended, elective, limited use, not recommended)—remains the foundation of how Internet standards are tracked and managed.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) maintains an official list of standards that define how the Internet's protocols work. The IAB coordinates this work with the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) to ensure Internet protocols evolve in a coordinated way. This coordination is essential because Internet protocols are now in widespread commercial use.

Protocols that aim to become standards go through a series of maturity levels with increasing amounts of scrutiny. When a protocol completes this process, it is assigned a STD number. At each step, the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) recommends advancement, and the IAB must ratify it. The IAB imposes minimum delays: at least six months before promotion from proposed to draft standard, and at least four months before promotion from draft to standard.

No proposed standard can advance to draft standard without at least two independent implementations and IESG recommendation. Moving from draft standard to standard generally requires operational experience and demonstrated interoperability between two or more implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: New protocols are like students going through school. They start as proposals, then become draft standards, then full standards if they work well. Each step requires testing and agreement from experts.

sections.title: Protocol Maturity Levels
sections.content:
Every protocol listed in RFC 1360 is assigned a maturity level or STATE of standardization:

Standard Protocol protocols have been established as official standards by the IAB and are assigned STD numbers. These are separated into two groups: IP-layer protocols that apply to the whole Internet, and network-specific protocols describing how to do IP on particular network types.

Draft Standard Protocol means the IAB is actively considering the protocol as a possible standard. Substantial and widespread testing is desired, and changes may occur before it becomes a standard.

Proposed Standard Protocol means the protocol is a proposal that may be considered by the IAB for standardization. Implementation and testing by several groups is desirable, and the specification is likely to be revised.

Experimental Protocol means a system should not implement it unless participating in the experiment and coordinating with the protocol developer. Experimental protocols are typically developed as part of ongoing research not intended for operational use, though they may eventually become proposed standards.

Informational Protocol means the protocol was developed by other standards organizations, vendors, or others outside the IAB's purview, but is published as an RFC for community convenience. Some may be recommended by the IAB.

Historic Protocol means the protocol is unlikely to ever become a standard because it has been superseded by later developments or lacks interest.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols have grades: Standard (official), Draft Standard (almost official), Proposed Standard (under review), Experimental (research only), Informational (published for reference), and Historic (old and replaced).

sections.title: Protocol Requirement Levels
sections.content:
In addition to maturity level, each protocol is assigned a requirement level or STATUS: Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, or Not Recommended.

Required Protocol means a system must implement it.

Recommended Protocol means a system should implement it.

Elective Protocol means a system may or may not implement it. The general rule is: if you are going to do something in that category, you must do exactly this. There may be several elective protocols in the same area (for example, several electronic mail protocols or several routing protocols).

Limited Use Protocol means the protocol is for use in limited circumstances. This may be because of its experimental state, specialized nature, limited functionality, or historic state.

Not Recommended Protocol means the protocol is not recommended for general use, possibly because of limited functionality, specialized nature, experimental state, or historic status.

The requirement level shown in RFC 1360 is sometimes only a one-word label that may not fully characterize implementation requirements in all situations. For some protocols, additional status paragraphs provide applicability statements. More detailed status information appears in separate requirements documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols also have priority levels: Required (must use), Recommended (should use), Elective (can use if needed), Limited Use (special cases only), and Not Recommended (avoid using).

sections.title: The Standards Track
sections.content:
Protocols progress along a formal standards track. The track diagram shows states in single-line boxes (temporary states where a protocol normally stays for several months) and double-line boxes (long-term states where a protocol may remain for years).

A protocol normally enters the standards track as a proposed standard. Generally, when entering the track, a decision is made about the eventual requirement level (elective, recommended, or required) the protocol will have, though a less stringent current status may be assigned initially.

The transition from proposed standard to draft standard requires the protocol to have been proposed standard for at least six months, and only the IAB can approve this on IESG recommendation. Moving from draft standard to standard requires at least four months in draft standard state, again with IAB approval on IESG recommendation.

Sometimes a protocol is assigned to the experimental state instead, which is off the standards track. Such protocols may be resubmitted to enter the standards track after further work. Other protocols become historic when they are replaced by another protocol or overtaken by other events.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols move through checkpoints: proposed, draft standard, then standard. Each step takes months of testing and agreement from leaders. Some protocols take a different path and become experimental or historic instead.

sections.title: Understanding the Protocol Lists
sections.content:
RFC 1360 contains lists of protocols organized by their maturity level and requirement level. These lists show which protocols are official standards, which are still being developed, and which are no longer recommended.

The document explains that while all standards are published as RFCs, not all RFCs specify standards. Anyone can submit an RFC, and submissions receive technical review as appropriate. The RFC Editor publishes documents describing proposed, draft, or standard protocols only with approval from both IESG and IAB. For experimental documents, the RFC Editor notifies IESG before publication.

A key principle is that once an RFC is assigned a number and published, that number is never revised or re-issued. However, a protocol may be improved and re-documented in several different RFCs. This is why RFC 1360 exists: to provide the authoritative reference for determining the correct, current RFC for each protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC list is the official source to check: for each protocol, which RFC has the current spec, whether it is official, and what level of requirement it has for different types of systems.
